children: companies are "over-earning," but surging corporate profits reflect a temporary acceleration rather than a dot-com-style "earnings bubble," according to Goldman Sachs.

S&P 500 EPS grew by an extraordinary 51% year-over-year in Q2 2026 and has risen 26% during the past four quarters—a pace exceeded only during post-recession rebounds in 2010 and 2021, Goldman wrote in a recent note to clients. This exceptional growth has pushed earnings well above their long-term trend and historical relationship with GDP growth.

While the cyclically-adjusted price-to-earnings ratio based on trailing 10-year earnings has climbed near record highs, the forward 12-month P/E multiple has actually declined from 23x a year ago to 19x today, matching its 10-year average.
Goldman identified three temporary factors driving the "over-earning" phenomenon. First, the AI
investment boom accounts for nearly half of S&P 500 EPS growth this year. Mega-cap hyperscalers

are on track to spend $800B on capex in 2026, up 94% from 2025; however, this tailwind is expected to fade as capex growth decelerates and depreciation expenses mount, transitioning from an 11 percentage point earnings boost this year to a marginal drag by 2028.
margins have expanded dramatically, with memory

firms enjoying gross margins near 80%—more than double their historical average. Goldman estimated margin expansion is driving about one-quarter of semiconductor earnings growth in 2026. If chip gross margins were to decline from 70% today to their 15-year average of 55%, it would cut S&P 500 earnings by roughly 10%, the note said.
Third, appreciating equity stakes are temporarily inflating earnings. Mega-cap tech companies

generated over $150B in "other income" from private investment gains in Q2 2026, accounting for 12% of S&P 500 EPS. Goldman expects this contribution to diminish significantly in 2027, creating an 8 percentage point drag on year-over-year growth comparisons.

Even with these headwinds, Goldman forecasted S&P 500 EPS growth of 11% in both 2027 (to $415) and 2028 ($460), supported by solid GDP growth and a growing boost from AI productivity gains estimated at 1-2 percentage points. The firm's 12-month S&P 500 target of 8,700 (+14%) reflects continued earnings growth as the main driver of the bull market.
